# Project background

This logbook narrates the analysis pipeline that supports the manuscript
*"Familial Correlation between Personality and Stress Exposure: Insights
from the Multigenerational Lifelines Cohort Study."* It is meant to be read
alongside the R scripts in this repository; every claim in the manuscript
can be traced to a code chunk here or to one of the numbered scripts.

The substantive question is: **how much of the variance in adult stress
exposure (childhood trauma, recent threatening events, ongoing
difficulties, loneliness, lack of social support) is shared across family
members, and how much of that familial covariance overlaps with the
familial component of three personality traits (Neuroticism, Extraversion,
Conscientiousness)?**

The answer comes from a multigenerational pedigree-based variance
decomposition (the classical ACE model) fitted in `ASReml-R`, with bivariate
extensions for every stress × stress and personality × stress pair.

# Phenotypes

Stress exposure (5 phenotypes, all from Lifelines questionnaires):

1. **Childhood trauma** — CTQ-SF (Bernstein et al., 1998; 25 clinical items,
   wave 2B). Sum score 25 – 125; dichotomised at the moderate Bernstein
   cut-off (≥ 40) for the liability-threshold heritability in script 04bc.
2. **List of Threatening Experiences (LTE)** — Brugha & Cragg (1990);
   12 binary events at four waves (1A, 1B, 1C, 2A). Combined across waves
   via a one-factor `lavaan` SEM with FIML.
3. **Long-term Difficulties Inventory (LDI)** — Rosmalen et al. (2012);
   9 domain items at the same four waves; same lavaan factor procedure.
4. **Loneliness** — De Jong Gierveld 6-item short form (wave 2B).
5. **Lack of social support** — SPF-IL Social Production Function
   Instrument for Level of Well-Being (Nieboer et al., 2005); 9 social-
   well-being items (wave 1A). The raw score is reversed so that "higher
   value = more stress".

Personality (3 traits from the Lifelines NEO release):

6. **Neuroticism** — NEO-PI-R 48-item six-facet domain sum (anxiety, anger-
   hostility, depression, self-consciousness, impulsiveness, vulnerability;
   6 × 8 items; range 48 – 240).
7. **Extraversion** — NEO-FFI domain SUM3 (11 items administered; one FFI
   item was omitted by Lifelines, so the Lifelines `SUM3` rule
   `round((SUM2 / NVALID) × 12)` rescales the score to a 12-item-equivalent
   12 – 60 analytic scale).
8. **Conscientiousness** — NEO-FFI domain SUM3 (12 items; 12 – 60).

All three personality variables are z-standardised before variance
decomposition (scripts 03, 05) so the raw-scale asymmetry across traits
does not affect estimates.

# The ACE model with `ASReml-R`

## Univariate (script 04)

For each phenotype *y* we fit a pedigree-based REML linear mixed model

$$y = \mu + \beta_1 \text{sex} + \beta_2 \text{age} + \beta_3 \text{age}^2 + a + c + e,$$

with `a ~ N(0, A * sigma_a^2)`, `c ~ N(0, I * sigma_c^2)` and
`e ~ N(0, I * sigma_e^2)`. *A* is the additive numerator relationship
matrix from the three-generation Lifelines pedigree, obtained via
`asreml::ainverse()`. One household level per residential `HouseID` provides
the shared-environment component.

```{r univariate-asreml, eval = FALSE}
library(asreml)

model <- asreml(
  fixed   = phenotype ~ sex + age + I(age^2),
  random  = ~ vm(PSEUDOIDEXT, Ainv) + HouseID,
  data    = baseline,
  na.action = na.method(x = "omit")
)

heritability <- vpredict(model, h2 ~ V2 / (V1 + V2 + V3))   # additive genetic
shared_env   <- vpredict(model, c2 ~ V1 / (V1 + V2 + V3))   # household
unique_env   <- vpredict(model, e2 ~ V3 / (V1 + V2 + V3))   # residual
```

`vpredict()` refers to variance parameters by their position in the
`vparameters` slot of the asreml object (`V1`, `V2`, …). The order is
**alphabetical by random-term name**, not the order written in the random
formula.

| Position | Variance component         | Interpretation |
|----------|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| `V1`     | `HouseID!HouseID.var`      | Shared household (*c²*) |
| `V2`     | `vm(PSEUDOIDEXT, Ainv)!ped`| Additive genetic (*h²*) |
| `V3`     | `units!R`                  | Residual / unique env (*e²*) |

Likelihood-ratio tests use `boundary = TRUE` to handle a variance fixed at
zero (50 : 50 mixture of $\chi^2_0$ and $\chi^2_1$).

## Bivariate (scripts 04, 05)

The two-trait extension stacks the two phenotypes in long format and gives
the additive genetic, shared-household and residual covariance an
unstructured 2 × 2 form (`us(trait)`). The four correlations of interest:

```{r bivariate-asreml, eval = FALSE}
rg <- vpredict(model, rg ~ V5 / sqrt(V4 * V6))                              # genetic
rc <- vpredict(model, rc ~ V2 / sqrt(V1 * V3))                              # shared env
re <- vpredict(model, re ~ V9 / sqrt(V8 * V10))                             # unique env
rp <- vpredict(model, rp ~ (V2 + V5 + V9) /
                          sqrt((V1 + V4 + V8) * (V3 + V6 + V10)))           # phenotypic
```

**Always** confirm the V-indexing before trusting a `vpredict()` call:

```{r vparam-check, eval = FALSE}
cbind(summary(model)$varcomp, n = seq_along(model$vparameters))
```

A forgotten `idv()` or an extra constraint silently shifts every subsequent
index and the correlation formula then estimates the wrong quantity.

# Item-level scoring (script `02a_score_construction.R`)

All stress measures use **mean-imputation when fewer than half of the
items in a subscale are missing**, except LTE and LDI, where items code
discrete events for which imputation is not theoretically defensible
(complete-case scoring per wave). The CTQ-SF reverse-coded items
(q2, q5, q7, q13, q19, q26, q28) are recoded `5↔1, 4↔2` before scoring.
SPF-IL is sign-flipped so that higher values mean more stress.

Personality scoring follows the canonical Lifelines / UGLI rule
`SUM3 = round((SUM2 / NVALID) × k)` with *k* = 8 for NEO-PI-R facet sums
and *k* = 12 for NEO-FFI domain sums. For Extraversion this single formula
serves two purposes at once: the systematically missing 12th NEO-FFI item
is imputed to the participant's mean of the 11 administered items, and any
further item-level missingness is mean-imputed by the same rule.

Cronbach's α for every multi-item stress scale is computed in
`02a_score_construction.R` Step 6 and written to
`output/tables/table_S7e_internal_consistency.tsv` (Suppl. Table S7e).
Published internal-consistency estimates from the Dutch NEO manuals 
(Hoekstra et al., 2007) provide background information on the psychometric 
properties of the instruments. Personality traits were assessed using 
the 48-item NEO-PI-R Neuroticism scale and the 12-item NEO-FFI 
Extraversion and Conscientiousness scales, as described in the Supplementary Methods.

# Cross-wave latent factors for LTE and LDI (script `02_data_preparation.R`)

LTE and LDI are administered at four assessment waves (1A, 1B, 1C, 2A).
Each pair of consecutive waves correlates around 0.4 – 0.6 (Suppl. Table
S5). Rather than analysing each wave separately, we fit a one-factor
congeneric CFA across waves with FIML missing-data handling in `lavaan`:

```{r lavaan-cfa, eval = FALSE}
library(lavaan)
model <- "F =~ LTE_1A + LTE_1B + LTE_1C + LTE_2A"
fit   <- sem(model, data = baseline, missing = "fiml", estimator = "ML")
baseline$LTE_latent <- as.numeric(predict(fit))
```

Factor scores are then standardised to SD = 1 in script 04 so the variance
components are interpretable on a unit-variance scale. Per-wave ACE
estimates (Suppl. Table S9, script `05b_perwave_univariate.R`) confirm
that any single wave has lower *h²* than the latent factor — exactly the
expected attenuation due to wave-specific measurement error, and the
practical justification for the latent-factor step.

# Inverse-normal-transformation sensitivity (script `05_sensitivity_int.R`)

ASReml assumes (multivariate) normality of the residuals. Childhood
trauma, LTE, LDI and Loneliness are right-skewed, with some discrete
spikes around mean-imputed integer values. We refit every univariate and
bivariate model with the rank-based inverse-normal transform

$$y_{\text{INT}} = \Phi^{-1}\!\bigl((\text{rank}(y) - 0.5) / n\bigr)$$

and report the comparison in Suppl. Table S10 and Suppl. Figs S19 – S20.
The qualitative pattern is unchanged.

# Liability-scale heritability for dichotomous childhood trauma (script `06_rrr_liability_heritability.R`)

For the dichotomous CT phenotype we additionally compute the
liability-scale heritability from the first-degree-relative recurrence
risk ratio (RRR), following the Wray & Gottesman (2012) liability-threshold
framework. The pipeline:

1. Estimate prevalence *K* in the unrelated sample.
2. For every proband-relative pair, compute the relative-conditional
   prevalence *λ*; the RRR is $\lambda / K$.
3. Map RRR back to a liability-scale *h²* using the bivariate-normal
   threshold model (Wray & Gottesman, 2012, Eq. 1; Bos et al., 2025).
4. Standard errors are clustered at the family level using the
   `sandwich` package (cluster-robust score CIs).

Subscale heritability (Suppl. Table S12b, script
`06b_ct_subscale_heritability.R`) is reported at both the moderate
Bernstein cut-off (`≥ 40`) and a low cut-off (`≥ 30`) so the reader can
judge the cut-off sensitivity.

# Multiple-testing policy

Two separate Bonferroni families are applied for the primary analyses:

| Family | Tests | α (Bonferroni) |
|--------|------:|---------------:|
| Univariate ACE (LRT for *h²* = 0) | 8 | .05 / 8 = .00625 |
| Bivariate ACE (per-pairing FWER) | 25 | .05 / 25 = .002  |

The bivariate correction is at the *pairing* level rather than the
*correlation* level (75 tests) because rg, rc and re from a single pairing
decompose the same rP from the same fit and share the same *N* (Visscher
et al., 2014; Yengo et al., 2018). Sensitivity and exploratory analyses
(INT, per-wave, CT-liability, CT-subscale, age-bracket) are not corrected
and are reported descriptively.

The `*_p` columns in Suppl. Tables S13 + S14 are two-sided normal-
approximation Wald p-values (`2 * pnorm(-|est / se|)`). Wald and LRT
p-values agree to ≥ 3 decimals away from variance-component boundaries
(rg ≈ ±1, c² ≈ 0).

# Interpretation: what bivariate correlations can and cannot show

The bivariate ACE decomposes the phenotypic correlation
$r_\text{P}$ between two traits into three additive parts:

$$r_\text{P} = r_g\sqrt{h^2_X h^2_Y} + r_c\sqrt{c^2_X c^2_Y} + r_e\sqrt{e^2_X e^2_Y}.$$

A non-zero *rg* tells us that the *familial* component of *X* overlaps with
the *familial* component of *Y*. It does **not** identify the substantive
mechanism: a shared additive-genetic component, vertical cultural
transmission, assortative mating, and shared-household assortment all
load onto *rg* in a pedigree-based design without genotyped variants.
The same caveat applies to *rc* (any factor that clusters by household,
including parental SES or proximate environment, contributes here) and
*re* (within-person correlation of residual error). The manuscript
Discussion §4 spells out the interpretive boundary; we list the
candidate mechanisms but do not claim to distinguish among them.
